summary: Full-ingestion audit of pages #9-#12 complete. All four pages read in full, plus overlap partners #2 (30-sudden-spike...), #15 (334w duplicate), #41 (draft), and #01 (electric-bill-reader). Verified 6 facts against live sources (retrieved 2026-08-29), flagged 8 claims UNVERIFIED/NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. Confirmed #9 slug-vs-body intent mismatch; #12 title '12 Common Causes' over-promises (body has no 12-cause list); mapped #12/#2 duplication and #15 absorption; mapped #11/#01/#41 overlap.
findings: PAGE #9 (05-how-to-lower-utility-bills, 68pv, 86s TOP): Frontmatter title is now honest — 'How to Prioritize Utility-Bill Improvements'. Body delivers a prioritization methodology (baseline, assessment, categorize problem, compare proposals, review with bill data) and explicitly says 'Do not start with a generic list of gadgets, thermostat settings, or promised savings.' The title does NOT over-promise 'lower utility bills'; the MISMATCH lives in the slug (05-how-to-lower-utility-bills), the description ('...prioritize... improvements'), the keywords (['lower utility bills',...]), and the live URL, all of which promise lowering bills. Fix: rename slug to a prioritization slug (e.g. 05-how-to-prioritize-utility-bill-improvements) with a redirect/alias from the old URL, update keywords; OR retitle to deliberately serve the 'lower utility bills' intent by adding a direct savings-priority summary near the Quick Answer. Body does contain dollar savings ranges in the improvement table, so it is not 'no savings content', but those numbers are national estimates and several rows lack sources.

PAGE #9 weak-copy/fact issues: 'EPA: average family saves $70/yr in water + energy[5]' — source [5] (epa.gov/watersense/start-saving) retrieved 2026-08-29 says average family spends $1,300/yr in water costs and can save $500 from retrofitting WaterSense fixtures + ENERGY STAR appliances; the $70/yr figure is NOT on that page → UNVERIFIED/NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. 'Reduces standby heat loss 25–45% per DOE' has no inline citation → NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. '3–5% savings per 10°F reduction' (water heater) no source → NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. '~$75/yr average at national electricity rates' for LEDs no source → NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. 'Duct losses 20–30% of heating/cooling energy[4]' — source [4] energy.gov/save/home-upgrades was fetched; visible text did not include the 20–30% duct figure → UNVERIFIED/NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. 'DOE: can reduce heating/cooling cost 10–20%[1]' — source [1] (energy.gov/public-services/homes/home-weatherization/home-energy-audits) returns HTTP 404 as of 2026-08-29 → DEAD LINK + unverified. Improvement table header admits 'typical ranges based on DOE data and national averages' — the $10–30/mo, $15–40/mo, payback ranges are unsourced estimates and are exactly the 'exact savings' credibility risk in the parent objective.

PAGE #9 verified: DOE Home Upgrades page (https://www.energy.gov/save/home-upgrades) confirms 'You can save as much as 10% a year on heating and cooling by simply turning your thermostat back 7°-10°F for 8 hours a day from its normal setting' — matches #9 [4] and #12 [5]. Product placement note: #9 embeds P3 Kill A Watt (B00009MDBU) and Emporia Vue 3 (B0C7B1LKDW) with nearly identical copy to #12's — duplicate affiliate placements.

PAGE #10 (23-utility-billing-cycle-explained, 65pv, 57s TOP): No intent mismatch; title 'How to Read the Billing Period on a Utility Statement' matches body. Key claims verified: EIA FAQ id=97&t=3 confirms 2022 US residential average 10,791 kWh/yr ≈ 899 kWh/month ≈ 29.6 kWh/day; HI 6,178/yr; LA 14,774/yr (used by #10 and #11). Con Edison bill FAQ confirms factors: 'More days in the billing period', 'Whether the current or previous bills were estimated', and supply price fluctuation — supporting #10's 'long-vs-short-month math' and estimated-read sections. UNVERIFIED specifics: '27–35 days', 'shifts 1–3 days', 'seasonal variation of 3–6 days' are presented as general facts with no source → needs a provider-specific citation or soften to 'can range'.

PAGE #10 overlap/fix: Quick Answer and the 'For help with a surprise spike, check [why your bill jumped](/blog/15-why-utility-bill-higher-same-usage/)' link point at #15, the page designated for absorption into #12 (03-why-is-my-electric-bill-so-high). After #15 is retired, retarget this link to /blog/03-why-is-my-electric-bill-so-high/. #10's billing-period-length analysis is the natural owner of that concept; #12 and #2 should link to #10 rather than re-derive it.

PAGE #11 (electric-bill-breakdown-understanding-line-items, 65pv, 56s TOP): Strong sourcing (EIA, ConEd, CPUC). VERIFIED: EIA FAQ id=97&t=7 confirms 2022 avg 10,791 kWh/yr, 899/mo, HI 6,178, LA 14,774. EIA Today in Energy id=65244 confirms monthly bills are 'product of two factors: retail electricity prices and the amount of grid-delivered electricity that customers consume.' Con Edison FAQ confirms 'supply, delivery, and taxes' charge structure. UNVERIFIED: '2025 average U.S. retail price ... about 13.63¢/kWh, residential ... about 17.30¢/kWh' and the derived '$155 for the supply portion' — the EIA prices-and-factors page was fetched but the 2025 rate table was not visible in the captured text; EIA data exists (2024 res avg was 16.5¢/kWh per id=65244) but the article's 2025 numbers need direct confirmation → NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. CPUC estimate-billing specifics (same-period-last-year estimates, >3 months notification) were not independently fetched → UNVERIFIED/NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW.

PAGE #11 overlap map: (a) vs #01 (01-how-to-read-your-electric-bill): both cover billing period, meter info (actual/estimated), rate-plan check, itemized charges, time-of-use/tiered, and comparison method. #01 is the line-by-line 'how to read' owner; #11 is the 'charge-category encyclopedia' owner → current cross-links are appropriate; #11's 'Charge Categories You May See' table and #01's 'Understand the Charges on Your Statement'/'Plain-English terms' tables are the main redundancy; recommend #11 keep category table, #01 keep question-driven table, and add one cross-reference sentence rather than duplicating. (b) vs #41 (41-how-to-read-electricity-bill.md): #41 is a draft (draft: true) with nearly identical concept to #01, and #01 already carries the alias /blog/41-how-to-read-electricity-bill/ → no live duplicate; the orphan draft should be deleted or converted to a redirect to #01 so it cannot be published accidentally.

PAGE #12 (03-why-is-my-electric-bill-so-high, 64pv, 31s TOP, 85.2% bounce): TITLE OVER-PROMISE — title is 'Why Is My Electric Bill So High? 12 Common Causes and How to Fix Them' but the body has NO enumerated 12-cause list (it has a 5-item comparison table, a 4-branch diagnosis sequence, and three investigation areas). This is a concrete accuracy/title-integrity defect; fix by either numbering the causes (rewrite the investigation sections as causes 1–12) or retitle to remove '12 Common Causes' (e.g. '...: Compare Usage, Rate, and Billing Factors'). LOW time-on-page (31s) is consistent with readers not finding the promised 12 causes.

PAGE #12 verified: EIA Today in Energy id=65244 (fetched 2026-08-29) confirms #12's Quick Answer framing — residential bills reflect both usage and retail price; also gives 2024 US avg residential price 16.5¢/kWh and avg monthly bill $144 (good replacement figure if #12 wants a current national anchor). DOE Home Upgrades page confirms thermostat 7–10°F/8hr 'as much as 10% a year' (used at [5]). UNVERIFIED/NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW in #12: RECS 2020 end-use data (source [4]), ENERGY STAR '90% more efficiently' LED claim (source [7]), bsesc heat-pump water heater claim (source [6]), and 'One kWh is one kilowatt used for one hour' (source [2], basic but not fetched).

PAGE #12 vs #2 (30-sudden-spike-electricity-bill-no-usage) overlap map: DUPLICATED in both: billing-period length; estimated-read correction; thermostat setback (DOE 10%); weather/HVAC working harder; HVAC filter maintenance; appliance load checks (space heater, water heater, pool, EV, dehumidifier); kWh=kW×hr formula; Kill A Watt + Emporia product boxes; 'don't assume meter error' advice. UNIQUE to #2: 12-step investigation procedure; circuit-by-circuit breaker test; 7-day self-meter read; meter test request ($5–$25); PUC escalation with ~30-day timeline; cross-billing/meter-number verification; electrical hazard list (short circuits, rodent damage, aluminum wiring); specific phantom-load kWh figures (1,500W heater 8h = ~360 kWh/mo $40–60; water heater 300–500 kWh; dehumidifier 200–400; EV 250–500; pool pump 300–500). UNIQUE to #12: 4-branch diagnosis sequence; utility-vs-electrician-vs-HVAC contact split; same-season year-ago comparison; Today/This-month action checklist; FAQ 'why high if similar kWh' (which is exactly #15's thesis). OWNERSHIP RECOMMENDATION: #12 = diagnostic/decision owner (what to compare, sequence, when to call); #2 = deep-dive operational owner (12-step runbook focused on 'no usage change' spikes). Reduce duplicate prose by making #2's steps link to #12 for the compare-and-diagnose method and #12 link to #2 for the spike runbook; keep appliance kWh numbers in #2 only.

PAGE #12 absorbs #15 (15-why-utility-bill-higher-same-usage, 334w): #15's content is already ~80% present in #12's Quick Answer/first table/FAQ. The one #15-unique element is the payment caveat: 'Do not withhold payment or assume a charge is incorrect before confirming the utility's review and dispute process.' Fix: add that exact caveat to #12's 'When to Contact the Utility' section before retiring #15; then retarget all inbound links to #15 (found: #10's Quick Answer; search shows /blog/15-why-utility-bill-higher-same-usage/ referenced) to /blog/03-why-is-my-electric-bill-so-high/ and add a #15 → #12 redirect/alias.

Cross-page/site leads for Commander: (1) all 4 pages cite inline [n] sources and have frontmatter sources, contradicting the '92/96 guides have zero outbound URLs' site fact — confirms only a subset of the corpus is source-less; audit should re-run per-page. (2) author identities: #9 David Chen, #10/#11 Margaret Harrington, #12/#2/#15 Tanya Patterson — substantiation pending (out of scope, recorded as cross-shard lead). (3) #9 and #12 duplicate product boxes should be deduplicated in remediation to avoid redundant affiliate placement.
